clinicalPearls: Overactive bladder is a symptom syndrome defined by urinary urgency, usually with frequency and nocturia, with or without urgency incontinence, in the absence of infection or other identifiable pathology.
Urgency, the sudden compelling desire to void that is difficult to defer, is the cornerstone symptom and distinguishes overactive bladder from the normal, deferrable urge to pass urine.
Detrusor overactivity on urodynamics is a related but separate concept; many patients with overactive bladder symptoms show no involuntary contractions, and the diagnosis remains clinical.
A bladder diary quantifying frequency, voided volumes, urgency episodes and fluid intake is the single most useful assessment tool and guides behavioural therapy.
First-line treatment is conservative: fluid and caffeine modification, bladder training and pelvic floor muscle training, before considering pharmacotherapy.
Pharmacological options include antimuscarinic agents and beta-3 adrenergic agonists; antimuscarinic anticholinergic load should be minimised in older and cognitively vulnerable patients.
Refractory cases may respond to intradetrusor botulinum toxin injection, percutaneous or sacral neuromodulation, always after excluding significant post-void residual and other pathology.

New or persistent overactive bladder symptoms in an older patient, or symptoms with visible haematuria, mandate exclusion of bladder carcinoma or carcinoma in situ before ascribing them to overactive bladder.
reference.pathophysiology: Overactive bladder reflects a disturbance of the storage phase of the micturition cycle in which afferent and efferent control of the detrusor is dysregulated. Proposed mechanisms include a myogenic component, with increased spontaneous detrusor activity and enhanced coupling between smooth muscle cells, and a neurogenic component, with heightened afferent signalling and reduced central inhibition of the voiding reflex. Urothelial and suburothelial signalling abnormalities, involving altered release of acetylcholine, ATP and other mediators and up-regulated receptor sensitivity, augment sensory input from the bladder wall. The net effect is a perception of urgency at low bladder volumes, often accompanied by phasic involuntary detrusor contractions during filling. Contributing factors include ageing, bladder outlet obstruction, metabolic and neurological disease, and pelvic floor dysfunction, but in most patients no single structural cause is identified.
additionalDifferentials: Urinary tract infection or bacterial cystitis
Bladder carcinoma or carcinoma in situ
Bladder outlet obstruction with secondary detrusor overactivity
Neurogenic detrusor overactivity from spinal or cerebral disease
Polyuria from diabetes, diuretics or excessive fluid intake
additionalInvestigations: Frequency-volume bladder diary over several days
Urinalysis and urine culture to exclude infection and haematuria
Post-void residual measurement by bladder ultrasound
Urine cytology when carcinoma in situ is suspected
Urodynamic study in refractory, complex or pre-surgical cases
Cystoscopy where haematuria, pain or malignancy risk is present
redFlags: Persistent sterile pyuria or recurrent proven infection
Significant post-void residual or palpable bladder suggesting retention
New neurological signs, back pain or lower limb symptoms suggesting a neurological cause
Rapidly progressive symptoms or bladder pain suggesting malignancy or bladder pain syndrome
reference.prognosis: Overactive bladder is a chronic, fluctuating condition rather than a curable one, but the majority of patients achieve meaningful symptom control and improved quality of life with a stepped combination of behavioural measures, pharmacotherapy and, where needed, minimally invasive therapies. Symptom relapse after stopping treatment is common.
pitfalls: Starting antimuscarinic therapy without excluding a large post-void residual, risking precipitation of retention
Labelling symptoms as overactive bladder without excluding infection, haematuria or malignancy
Ignoring cumulative anticholinergic burden and cognitive risk in elderly patients
Overlooking modifiable contributors such as caffeine, excessive evening fluids or constipation
Failing to recognise bladder pain syndrome, in which pain rather than urgency drives frequency
references: European Association of Urology Guidelines on non-neurogenic female lower urinary tract symptoms
International Continence Society standardisation of terminology
